attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter. He is not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: The draft keeps both causal parts: GPU buying did little for revenue until the labs scaled, and it pumped stock values. It drops the side remark that Wall Street credited all revenue to AI, which is acceptable. 'Hyperscaler' stands in for Microsoft, Google and Amazon.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary. The 2022 to publication window fits the context. The contract flags the missing threshold and the missing date for when the labs became big enough. Its causal standard is demanding but follows from the speaker's causal wording.

evidence.note: Microsoft says AI added about 1 point to Azure growth in Q2 2023, so it was small early on. This is one company and one quarter, with no split between OpenAI and other customers and no GPU attribution.
Microsoft shares fell 3.6% premarket after it announced AI spending plans. A single-day reaction says little about the cumulative valuation effect either way.

reviews.rationale: The evidence has no customer-level revenue attribution and no causal estimate of how GPU spending affected valuations. The Microsoft 2023 figure fits a small early AI contribution but does not separate lab spending. The one-day stock drop cannot settle the valuation part. Neither element can be established or rejected.

attribution.note: Zitron's own firm assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Saying the 'paying off' claimants were wrong commits him to AI not having paid off. The draft renders this faithfully. 'Well-spent' is partly an evaluative judgment, but it has a financial component that can be checked.

contract.note: The plain reading, returns commensurate with costs, is ordinary. Using the Apr–Jun 2026 quarter is the drafter's choice: the speaker's claim covers capex since 2022. The contract correctly says interpretation determines the result.

evidence.note: Meta discloses an AI-driven conversion gain. It gives no incremental profit and no matched capital cost, so it shows a benefit but not an adequate return.
Microsoft says new Azure capacity was quickly monetized. This is not isolated to AI and is not net of costs.
Amazon attributes higher capex mainly to AI over the trailing twelve months, which is a cost signal. It gives no AI return figure for the target quarter.

reviews.rationale: All three items are company disclosures that show some AI benefits and large AI capex. None matches AI-attributable profit against capital cost at any of the four companies. The evidence neither shows inadequate returns at all four nor adequate returns at any one. The evidence cannot settle it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The firm 'will require' and 'will not meet' wording is kept. The antecedent (labs falling short of the revenue level) and the four-year horizon are kept.

contract.note: Reading revenue as realized annual revenue is ordinary. The contract flags whether the comparison is combined or per company and which expectations metric applies. The August 2030 deadline matches 'next four years'.

evidence.note: Microsoft beat its own guidance for the June 2026 quarter. That is an earlier period and management guidance, not the future expectations the forecast concerns.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is August 2030, after the evaluation date. Whether the antecedent occurs (labs short of the revenue level within four years) cannot be known yet. No conclusive early event is in the packet. The forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own concluding assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The antecedent and the named companies are kept. 'When they fail' could suggest he expects the failure itself. Reading it as conditional is reasonable but leaves that implied expectation unscored.

contract.note: The readings of 'hypergrowth ends' and 'apocalyptic' (severe distress) are ordinary, and the contract declines to import a deadline. It is labelled 'retrospective' although the claim is prospective, a minor labelling error.

evidence.note: Anthropic's S-1 risk factor says its compute obligations may outrun revenue. It describes a contingent risk, not a realized inability to spend, and covers only one of the two labs.

reviews.rationale: Nothing shows that either lab has been unable to finance compute spending on the stated scale, so the antecedent is unknown. No deadline was given, and no conclusive event meets the early-resolution rule. A risk disclosure does not establish that the antecedent occurred, so the forecast cannot be scored.
